manual.title: Caregiver Manual & Stress Relief
manual.subtitle: Comprehensive strategies, de-escalation protocols, and well-being tools for dementia caregivers in NER.

guide.title: 1. Daily Routine & Schedule Synchronization
guide.text: Maintain consistent mealtime and activity schedules.

deescalation.title: 1. Managing Sundowning & Agitation
deescalation.text: Reduce ambient sensory stimuli and initiate calm background audio.

whatIs.title: What Is Dementia?
whatIs.text: Dementia is an umbrella term for a decline in memory, thinking, and reasoning skills severe enough to interfere with daily life. It is caused by damage to brain cells and is progressive, meaning symptoms generally worsen over time. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form, accounting for a majority of cases.

earlySigns.title: Common Early Signs
earlySigns.text: Frequent memory lapses, difficulty finding words, confusion about time or place, trouble planning familiar tasks, and noticeable changes in mood or personality are often among the first signs families notice.

stages.title: The Three Broad Stages
stages.early: Mild forgetfulness and occasional confusion; the person is usually still independent.
stages.middle: Memory gaps grow, help is needed with daily tasks, and wandering or repeating questions is common.
stages.late: Significant loss of ability to communicate and carry out basic activities; full-time care is typically required.

detection.title: Why Early Detection Matters
detection.text: There is currently no cure, but early diagnosis allows families to plan care, start supportive therapies, adjust routines, and access medications that can slow symptom progression in some cases.

supporting.title: Supporting a Person with Dementia
supporting.text: Consistent routines, a calm and well-lit environment, patience during communication, and regular cognitive engagement (such as memory games and social interaction) can meaningfully improve quality of life for both patients and caregivers.

tips.title: Dementia Care Tips & Articles
tips.subtitle: Practical guidance families and caregivers can apply at home:

nutrition.title: Nutrition & Diet
nutrition.text: Offer small, frequent meals with familiar regional foods. Keep water visible and accessible throughout the day, as thirst cues are often forgotten. Limit sugary and heavily processed snacks, and favor finger foods if using utensils becomes difficult.

activity.title: Physical Activity
activity.text: Short daily walks, light stretching, or simple household chores help maintain mobility and improve mood. Aim for gentle, consistent movement rather than intense exercise, and always supervise outdoor activity.

sleep.title: Sleep & Sundowning
sleep.text: Keep a consistent bedtime routine, limit caffeine after noon, and use dim, warm lighting in the evening. If confusion or agitation increases at dusk, calm music and a familiar face nearby can help ease the transition.

safety.title: Home Safety
safety.text: Remove loose rugs and clutter, install grab bars near the bathroom, label rooms clearly, and keep sharp objects, medicines, and cleaning supplies locked away or out of reach.

communication.title: Communication
communication.text: Use short, simple sentences and maintain eye contact. Give the person time to respond, avoid quizzing their memory, and focus on the feeling behind their words rather than correcting every detail.

support.title: Support Groups & Community
support.subtitle: Caregivers don't have to manage alone — these are the kinds of support worth seeking out in the NER:

local.title: Local Caregiver Support Groups
local.text: Many district hospitals and NGOs run periodic caregiver meet-ups where families share coping strategies and practical advice. Ask your nearest medical center (see the Care Directory) whether one operates in your area.

organizations.title: National & Regional Dementia Organizations
organizations.text: Bodies such as the Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India (ARDSI) run chapters and helplines across India, offering counseling, day-care referrals, and caregiver training resources.

online.title: Online Communities
online.text: Moderated online forums and social media groups for dementia caregivers can offer round-the-clock peer support, especially useful for families in remote areas with limited access to in-person groups.

mentalHealth.title: Mental Health Support for Caregivers
mentalHealth.text: Caregiver burnout is common and real. The Tele-MANAS helpline (14416) offers free, confidential psychological support for caregivers as well as patients, 24/7.

reportsGuide.title: Understanding Your Reports
reportsGuide.description: What score, accuracy, and session counts on the Reports tab actually mean.
reportsGuide.sessionsText: How many times a patient has played a given game. More sessions generally mean more consistent engagement.
reportsGuide.scoreText: A game-specific point total. Compare a patient's own scores over time rather than against other patients — the goal is their personal trend.
reportsGuide.accuracyText: The share of correct responses in a session. A gradual dip across several sessions is worth mentioning at their next check-up; a single low session usually isn't.
reportsGuide.watchForText: Sudden drops, not gradual ones, matter most — they're more likely to reflect an off day (poor sleep, discomfort) than a real change.

faq.title: NeuroPlay Help & FAQ
faq.description: How login codes work, adding a patient, and what online/offline status means.
faq.loginCodeText: A short code your patient enters on their device to open their own dashboard. Each code expires after a set time for security.
faq.codeExpiresText: Use "Regenerate Code" on the patient's card in the Patients tab. This invalidates the old code immediately.
faq.onlineOfflineText: Online means that patient's dashboard is currently open on their device. It updates in real time as they log in or out.
faq.addPatient: How do I add a patient?
faq.addPatientText: Select "Add Patient" from the dashboard overview. You'll get a Patient ID and login code to share with them.

glossary.title: Dementia Glossary
glossary.description: Plain-language definitions for terms you'll see in care notes and reports.
glossary.sundowningText: Increased confusion or agitation in the late afternoon and evening.
glossary.cognitiveDeclineText: A gradual reduction in memory, reasoning, or thinking skills over time.
glossary.caregiverBurnoutText: Physical and emotional exhaustion from sustained caregiving, often with reduced patience or motivation.
glossary.reminiscenceTherapyText: Using familiar memories, photos, or music to support engagement and mood.
glossary.validationApproachText: Responding to the emotion behind what someone says, rather than correcting the facts.

manual.title: Caregiver Manual & Stress Relief
manual.description: Monitoring guides and anxiety de-escalation steps for hard moments.
manual.dailyRoutineText: Keep mealtimes and activities consistent. Mornings tend to bring the most cognitive clarity — a good window for memory exercises and light movement.
manual.managingSundowningText: Reduce noise and bright light in the late afternoon. Validate emotions rather than correcting facts, and redirect toward calm, familiar activities.
manual.breathingResetText: Box breathing: inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. Repeat for two to five minutes whenever things feel like too much.

tips.title: Dementia Care Tips
tips.description: Practical guidance on nutrition, sleep, home safety, and everyday communication.
tips.nutritionText: Small, frequent meals with familiar foods. Keep water visible, since thirst cues are often forgotten.
tips.sleepText: A consistent bedtime routine and dim evening lighting help. Calm music can ease dusk confusion.
tips.homeSafetyText: Remove loose rugs, add grab bars near the bathroom, and keep medicines and sharp objects out of reach.
tips.communicationText: Short, simple sentences. Give time to respond, and focus on the feeling behind the words rather than correcting every detail.
